item.title: Tribal Justice: Congressional Action Needed to Support Tribal Sovereignty
item.description:
What GAO Found
Tribes and the federal government generally share jurisdiction over certain crimes committed in Indian country. However, Tribes in states subject to Public Law 280 (P.L. 280) generally share criminal jurisdiction in Indian country with their respective state when a tribal citizen commits a crime or, in certain circumstances, is the victim of a crime.
Percent of Federally Recognized Tribes Located in the Lower 48 States
Tribes and states exercise criminal jurisdiction under P.L. 280 in various ways. For example, some Tribes and local law enforcement agencies have entered into cross-deputization agreements. These agreements generally provide tribal police officers with the same or similar jurisdiction and related authorities as local law enforcement officers within and outside of Indian country.
Further, some states have returned the criminal jurisdiction provided by P.L. 280 to the federal government (known as retrocession). Tribal leaders and state law enforcement officials provided various perspectives on retrocession. For example, tribal leaders told GAO retrocession helped enhance their Tribe’s exercise of self-determination and addressed some challenges working with state law enforcement. State law enforcement officials said that retrocession can be a challenge because Tribes would lose access to state public safety and justice services. However, under federal law, Tribes cannot initiate retrocession and tribal consent is not required when states do so. In the absence of amendments to address this, the law impedes Tribes’ exercise of self-determination.
In the lower 48 states, Tribes named in the law may face limitations in accessing certain funding for public safety and justice. GAO’s analysis of funding data from the Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) showed that from fiscal years 2017 through 2021, Tribes in states named in P.L. 280 received less funding per capita than Tribes in all other states. BIA officials stated that they have limited discretionary funding and generally prioritize funding for Tribes that do not receive public safety and justice services from their respective states.
Why GAO Did This Study
In 1953, P.L. 280 rescinded most federal criminal jurisdiction in Indian country in select states and instead provided it to these states. As of October 2026, approximately 65 percent of the 575 federally recognized Tribes were located in these states. Some prior research on the effect of P.L. 280 suggests the law may have adverse effects on public safety and justice, including slow police response times and limited access to certain federal funding.
GAO was asked to review the law’s effect on tribal public safety and justice. GAO previously issued a report on P.L. 280’s effect on tribal public safety and justice in Alaska.
This report examines the extent to which the law affects how jurisdiction is exercised in the continental United States, excluding Alaska (lower 48 states) and what federal research and data show about P.L. 280’s effect on Tribes in the lower 48, among other things. GAO analyzed relevant laws and federal memoranda on tribal jurisdiction, as well as federal crime and funding data for fiscal years 2017 through 2024—the most recent data available. GAO interviewed BIA and DOJ officials, non-governmental stakeholders and legal scholars, as well as tribal leaders and state law enforcement officials from three states subject to P.L. 280 in the lower 48 states.
